works.name: When You're in Love with a Beautiful Woman

podcast.title: Formation (Circa 1967)
podcast.body: The band started around the same time Rolling Stone magazine did, in 1967. They were initially a "rag tag bunch of musicians in a bar band," mostly from New Jersey. "Dr hook in the medicine show which started around the same time that rolling stone did was really still just a rag tag bunch of musicians in a bar band most of them from new jersey."

podcast.title: Streaking Performance (1974)
podcast.body: During their European tour in 1974, the band engaged in the streaking craze, stripping naked and running across the stage in Copenhagen, demonstrating their unrefined and anti-showbiz attitude. "They were compelled to engage in our favorite 1974 craze streaking as they stripped naked and ran across the stage in Copenhagen when they were on their uh european tour."

podcast.title: Name Change (Circa 1975)
podcast.body: The band simplified their name to simply Dr. Hook, starting around 1975, and went on to achieve significant success with soft rock hits. "The band which would simply go by Dr. Hook I think starting in 1975 would go on to big things too."

podcast.title: Anti-Showbiz Ethos
podcast.body: Lead singer Dennis Locoreer described the band's approach as avoiding flashy poses or showbiz. They developed their performance style by making up songs and voices during long drives between gigs, aiming for a "loose feeling" on stage to entertain themselves and the audience. "We were told if we could get that loose feeling on stage and forget about showbiz then we could have fun and entertain the audience at the same time."

podcast.title: Association with Shel Silverstein
podcast.body: Shel Silverstein was the writer for Dr. Hook & The Medicine Show, known for his diverse career as an author, illustrator, and songwriter. He wrote many of their songs, including comedic ones. "He was also the writer for dr hook in the medicine show."

podcast.title: Perceived "Dr. Hook" Identity
podcast.body: The band's look was shaggy and unrefined, contrasting with the more polished Shel Silverstein. Silverstein, with an eye patch due to an accident, was sometimes mistaken for the "Dr. Hook" of the band due to his pirate-like appearance. "He was presumed to be the dr hook of the band because he kind of looked like a pirate too."
